description: ASTRA I-CATS builds tools that make complex space data understandable. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we created LUNA NAV: one intuitive console where mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar landing sites, read Sun and Earth visibility, and see the terrain behind every decision. We pair scientific rigor with plain language, accessible design, and interactive visuals; turning SPICE ephemerides and LOLA terrain into a clear path from curiosity to a defensible decision.
summary: One-day delay in the launch schedule of a south-pole lunar mission changes everything. ASTRA LUNA NAV gives you this insight instantly. ASTRA LUNA NAV is a web console that will accelerate and optimize the process of planning a south-pole lunar mission. This planning process is complex since engineers should manage extreme conditions of lighting and communication blackouts while scientists are trying to detect volatiles in permanent shadow. Modern software is effective yet cumbersome, and comparison of scenarios takes an enormous amount of time despite the fact that even small changes in launch schedule or landing location can lead to significant changes in the results. ASTRA LUNA NAV resolves this problem. This console provides users with instantly comprehensible insights from 5-meter LOLA digital elevation model and SPICE DE440 ephemeris. Users can select either predefined or user-defined coordinates, change the dates of mission, and receive the information about the position of Sun and Earth with respect to the horizon line. Mission planners receive the explainable Mission Advisor, first-person surface visualization, power and communication timelines, side-by-side comparison, and report export. Educators get an Educator Lab that brings polar engineering challenges into the classroom. The public gets a chance to look into the process of lunar exploration. ASTRA LUNA NAV turns "what-if" into insight, helping teams pivot faster and opening the lunar south pole to everyone.
details:
We kept coming back to one question: Why is it still so hard to answer a simple lunar mission-planning question? If we want to know whether a lander can touch down near Shackleton Crater on a given date, generate power and keep a direct line to Earth, we should not need three tools, a spreadsheet and twenty minutes of cross-referencing.

That friction is what my team set out to remove with ASTRA LUNA NAV, a browser-based lunar landing-site navigator and mission-planning console for the Moon’s south pole. It lets mission designers, researchers, educators and the public compare candidate sites and landing dates side by side.

What It Does and How It Works

ASTRA LUNA NAV guides users through a four-step wizard:
1.choose a mission profile
2.pick a site (catalog or custom lat/lon)
3.choose a landing date


4.review a mission summary. (you will get this pdf report with just single button)


The console then opens into three physics-driven lenses:

  • Terrain: An interactive LOLA DEM map with site markers, slope/illumination/line-of-sight rasters, 2D horizon profiles and a 3D site view from real elevation data.
  • Sun & Earth Position & Info

This view is our telemetry engine. It calculates exact ephemerides like Azimuth, Elevation and Distance, and it is for both the Sun and Earth. It translating them into real-time engineering metrics like solar array output (W/m²) and link margin (dB). As the image shows, the Local Sky View plots their 24-hour paths while our Visibility Timeline maps a 14-day window in 10-minute increments. The color-coding lets planners instantly spot windows where both are visible (green), Sun-only (yellow), or Earth-only (blue).

  • Sun & Earth visibility: Sun elevation/azimuth, Earth line-of-sight, illumination percentage, eclipse indicators, a sky/orrery view from SPICE-style ephemerides and a timeline scrubber with sunrise, sunset and Earth-Set/Rise events.
  • Mission Advisor: An automated scoring engine that evaluates each site/date against a selected mission profile including Artemis scouting, commercial ice run and geology traverse. It will return a GO / CONDITIONAL / NO-GO verdict with named constraint evidence for power, thermal, comms, lighting and slope.

Tailored Modes for Every Audience:

  • Educator Lab: A live sandbox where teachers can adjust Sun elevation sliders, see shadow cross-sections, and manipulate scoring weights (Safety vs. Power vs. Comm) to teach the physics behind the math.
  • Public View: A cinematic, plain-language first-person view. We included a 5-question interactive Moon Challenge with a "Mission Badge" system, turning planetary science into an engaging game.

Benefits

ASTRA LUNA NAV democratizes mission trade studies which once required bespoke SPICE scripting and GIS tooling, now it becomes point-and-click in a browser. It explains the “why” behind a site by decomposing verdicts into named constraints instead of a black-box score. It is multi-audience by design, with separate lenses for planners, educators and public. It is accessibility-conscious, with a colorblind-safe palette, keyboard controls, reduced-motion support and responsive layout. And it is reproducible, with data sources, formulas and validation tables documented in-app.

Intended Impact

We want ASTRA LUNA NAV to lower the barrier to rigorous lunar south-pole site selection for Artemis-era operations and to turn that same data into an engaging public and educational experience. The south pole is scientifically priceless but operationally hostile: Sun angles skim the horizon, Earth dips behind crater rims and slopes can exceed lander limits. If more people can evaluate those tradeoffs quickly and transparently, mission planning gets faster, public understanding gets deeper and science and engineering teams can coordinate around a shared picture.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software

To balance instant accessibility with scientific rigor, we architected ASTRA LUNA NAV in two modes: a zero-dependency static demo for immediate viewing and a full live API pipeline for dynamic ephemeris and DEM computation.

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript (ES2020). We used Canvas 2D for maps and trade charts, and WebGL for the 3D globe and terrain views. The static demo is a single self-contained file with no build step, designed for offline robustness.
  • Backend & Data Pipeline: Python 3.10+ and FastAPI. We used spiceypy for ephemerides and standard geospatial libraries for projecting LOLA DEM tiles. Node 18+ is used for the frontend build pipeline.
  • Testing: pytest ensures analytic horizon checks and API contract validation.
  • Reproducibility (Build Steps): For the live API, we built a transparent four-step pipeline. From the project root (pip install -r requirements.txt), the commands are:
    1. python scripts/fetch_data.py: Downloads SPICE kernels and LOLA DEM tiles (~420 MB) into the local cache. (It fails loudly if a kernel is missing, rather than silently substituting).
    2. python -m lunanav.build: Projects the DEMs and generates the 1,440-bin horizon grids and far-field blocking angles.
    3. pytest -q: Runs analytic horizon checks and API contract tests.
    4. ./run.ps1: Launches the FastAPI server and serves the console.

We built it this way because mission planners deserve a tool that is both instantly accessible and scientifically auditable. The static demo proves the concept in a browser, while the live API pipeline shows exactly how the physics and terrain calculations are computed from raw kernels.

How It Is Creative

The biggest creative choice was framing the advisor as the product, not the dashboard. Most lunar tools are data viewers; we built a mission-planning console with verdict badges and applied-mission state. Our split POV mode shows Sun and Earth simultaneously in first person from the landing site, the most intuitive way we know to explain why polar sites matter. Role-based onboarding reshapes the interface, not just a theme. The public story mode with a quiz makes mission design genuinely fun for non-experts.

Factors We Considered

We weighed scientific defensibility (explicit, tunable constraints and transparent scoring), offline reliability (zero external dependencies), multi-role usability (one engine for experts and public), accessibility (colorblind-safe palette, reduced motion, keyboard operability), in-browser performance (Canvas/WebGL over heavyweight frameworks) and auditability (validation KPIs and reproducible formulas in-app). We also learned to be honest about gaps: the build is feature-dense, the LOLA/SPICE provenance needs clearer labeling, and the WebGL globe needs a fallback. I would rather name those gaps than pretend they do not exist, honesty about approximations is what makes a tool trustworthy.

ASTRA LUNA NAV is a hackathon project, but we built it like we meant it. We am proud of what my team made, not just the code, but the judgment behind it: the choice to explain rather than obscure, to include rather than exclude, and to treat the Moon’s edge as a place worth understanding.
